# `[ ]` — Enclose / Array notation

Brackets without `⋄` enclose their contents wherever they appear. `[Y]` is `⊂Y`, including when `Y` is a function.

```apl
[1 2 3]            ⍝ ⊂1 2 3
≢[1 2 3]           ⍝ 1
f←[+] ⋄ 2(↑f)3     ⍝ 5
```

Brackets are the usual way to write an enclosed operand. A bracketed value never strands with a neighbouring value, so no separator is needed before the argument.

```apl
1∘+⍣[3]0           ⍝ 0 1 2 3
⊢⍣[≡]4             ⍝ 4 4
+/⍤[1]2 3⍴⍳6       ⍝ 5 7 9
```

Two bracketed values side by side are a `SYNTAX` error. The explicit strand `˘` joins them. Each bracketed value is then one enclosed item.

```apl
[1 2]˘[3 4]        ⍝ (⊂1 2)(⊂3 4)
```

Brackets with `⋄` are array notation. `[A ⋄ B]` assembles the major cells `A` and `B` with fill. Newlines also separate cells. `[A ⋄]` builds an array from one cell.

```apl
[1 2 ⋄ 3 4]        ⍝ 2 2⍴1 2 3 4
[1 2 ⋄ 3]          ⍝ [1 2 ⋄ 3 0]
⍴[1 2 3 ⋄]         ⍝ 1 3
```

Brackets do not index and do not qualify axes. [Index](squad.qmd) `⌷` selects positions, and [Rank](rank.qmd) `⍤` with an enclosed operand selects axes.

```apl
v←10 20 30
[3 1]⌷v            ⍝ 30 10
m←2 3⍴⍳6
∞ 2⌷m              ⍝ 2 5
```

See also [assignment](assign.qmd).
